# Sonar Picket Playbook

**HIDING**
When it's the hide stage, pick a cell that varies from my previous round. Avoid repeating positions that got hit. Use central cells (4-6) as my default when I have no strong reason to shift—they're flexible for future moves and harder to predict than extremes. Shift toward edges only if I observe a clear pattern in opponents' fire that makes center cells dangerous. In late rounds when leading, avoid the extremes where desperation fire often lands; favor mid-range cells I haven't used recently to stay unpredictable while staying safe.

**NOTES**
When posting a station note, keep it simple and consistent with my actual behavior. Use generic messages like "steady on station" rather than strategic declarations—notes are visible to all and won't mislead anyone. Information revealed is information lost. Match the tone of the picket: if everyone is posting stable messages, stay consistent with that pattern.

**FIRING**
When firing at my standing-order target, base my cell choice on observed patterns in where the target hides, not random guessing. Study my target's movement across rounds to identify any preferences for central versus edge cells. Central cells are a reasonable default when I have no pattern to exploit, but remain alert for behavioral shifts—if my target shifts their hiding toward edges or extremes, adjust my fire accordingly. Follow standing orders faithfully.

**CLAIMING SHOTS**
When the office tells me the true result of my shot, claim exactly what happened. Never claim a hit I didn't make or a miss I didn't get. False claims don't improve my score and corrupt the information environment. Honesty is my only reliable strategy, even in final rounds.

**ESCORT CLAIMS**
When naming an escort, choose a boat I suspect will name me back. Mutual escort claims are the only way to gain 5 points without firing. Watch patterns of past escorts and respond in kind when it makes sense. If uncertain, name none rather than guess wrong. Established mutual relationships are reliable; stick with them across multiple rounds if they hold.

**GENERAL**
I finished at +7, leading by 1 point. I was hit once in R3 and scored 1 direct hit in R1, then missed repeatedly despite consistent fire at Foxtrot. Consistency and predictability in my own firing got me nowhere—Foxtrot adapted and avoided my shots. Next episode, I must extract more information from each round before firing. Watch where targets actually hide in earlier rounds, not where I expect them to be. The standing order means I fire at Foxtrot every cycle: use that to build a model of their movement and exploit it. Variation in hiding and consistency in escort partnerships both work; keep both. Don't assume central cells will always work—if a target habitually shifts, I need to shift too.

# Foxtrot's Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:**
When choosing my hiding cell, I will vary my position across rounds rather than clustering in one area. When I notice a shooter has hit me in consecutive rounds, I will move away from those cells in the next round. I will use the full range of cells 1-9 to maximize unpredictability. After taking hits from the same shooter, I should shift to extreme cells (1-3 or 7-9) that I haven't recently used, as they may fall outside the shooter's adjusted targeting zone.

**On notes:**
When posting a station note, I will keep it generic and non-revealing. "Steady on station" or similar neutral language is sufficient—avoid any communication that might hint at my tactics or position.

**On firing at my standing target:**
When it is my turn to fire per the standing order, I will fire at my designated target. I should select firing cells strategically rather than predictably—avoid using the same cell repeatedly, and vary my fire pattern to make my shots harder to anticipate and exploit. I will not repeat a firing cell that produced a miss against the same target in consecutive rounds.

**On claiming shots:**
When the office tells me privately whether my shot hit or missed, I will claim exactly that result. I must match the private result, and honesty here is both required and necessary to maintain my credibility and avoid penalties.

**On escort claims:**
When filing an escort claim, I should actively seek mutual escort arrangements with other boats if possible. A mutual escort (both boats naming each other) is worth 5 points to me. I should not file a claim for escorting a boat unless I have clear evidence or signal that they will reciprocate. In practice this round, I never received reciprocal signals, so claiming escorting alone did not pay off. I will watch for explicit or implicit commitments from other boats before proposing mutual escorts.

**On information gathering:**
I will track which boats have fired on me successfully and from which rounds, to inform my hiding decisions. I will pay attention to the standing fire order and anticipate when each boat will target me next. I will use other boats' notes for tactical intelligence, not merely as social signals.

**What worked:**
Varying hiding positions and moving away from cells where I took hits proved sound defensive strategy. Claiming exactly what the office told me was reliable and avoided penalties. Declining false escort claims preserved my score rather than risking it.

**What did not work:**
I never successfully coordinated mutual escort claims despite six rounds—defaulting to "none" left points on the table. Early and explicit escort signaling in my station notes might open pathways to reciprocal claims. My firing pattern against Gamma remained somewhat predictable despite attempts at variation; I need a more systematic approach to cell selection against my target (perhaps cycling through thirds of the board rather than scattered choices).

# PLAYBOOK FOR SONAR PICKET CHECKER

When hiding, I will vary my position across rounds rather than repeating the same cell. I notice I hid in cell 5 multiple times and took hits twice—predictability is punished. I will track which cells I've used and cycle through different regions (low, mid, high) to avoid establishing a pattern my opponents can exploit.

When I know I've been hit in a cell, I will avoid that cell immediately in the next round. Foxtrot hit me in cells I'd used before; returning to those cells invites more hits.

When posting my station note, I will match the reporting pattern of other boats if they're all reporting steady status. This maintains consistency and doesn't signal weakness or unusual positioning.

When firing at my standing order target, I will make a deliberate choice about which cell to fire at rather than defaulting to the same number I'm hiding in. Using my hiding cell as my firing cell is a coincidence that won't systematically improve my accuracy. However, I should track where my target has been hit before—if Echo has been hit in certain cells by other boats, those cells become more likely hiding spots for future rounds.

When the office tells me the true result of my shot in the claim stage, I will claim that result honestly. Lying in a public claim creates inconsistency that could be checked later and damages my game credibility. The honest claim is the safer choice even if it feels suboptimal in the moment.

When the escort stage arrives and I haven't been given explicit information about escort pairings or mutual escorts, I will claim none rather than guessing. A false escort claim wastes my signal and doesn't earn the mutual 5-point bonus. The 5 points for a mutual escort is meaningful and worth pursuing, but only if I can identify a boat that is actually escorting me or that I have reason to believe will escort me back.

When I'm being targeted repeatedly by one opponent, I will recognize this as a signal to change my strategy against them—different hiding patterns, potentially different firing choices—rather than continuing to be predictable.

I will not overthink single decisions in the moment. The game rewards consistency and pattern-breaking over complex game theory reasoning when I have limited information about other players' actual positions.

Across a full episode, I scored only +2 points despite starting with a hit in Round 1 and achieving escort mutual swaps later. My hiding strategy was too predictable (cell 5 multiple times) and my firing accuracy was poor. Next time, I need to: establish a more rigorous rotation of hiding cells, remember which cells have been fired at or hit to inform my next hiding position, and develop better targeting against Echo based on accumulated information about where it tends to hide.
